speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of the presence in our country of an official trade mission from Cuba. The question is, does the government propose to control in any way the export of strategic materials to that country?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as strategic materials are concerned, the course to be followed will be that followed in other similar cases, namely that the strategic nature thereof shall at all times be taken into consideration.
I think I should add that the presence of a group from Cuba to which the hon. member refers does not mean that the Canadian government will fix or determine the volume of trade between Canada and that country, because Canada is not a state trading country. The opportunities for normal trade exist, and the outcome of the trade mission, subject of course to strategic materials, will depend on the decisions of individual Canadian businessmen and the prospective purchasers.

May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question arising out of the Prime Minister's reply to my question a moment ago. Is it the intention of the government to include Cuba in the list of countries to which export controls are applied in respect of strategic materials?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: There is no change contemplated with regard to export control at the present time, or to provide for other than the export controls which have been in existence in the past.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED REJECTION BY B.C. OF FINANCIAL CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
In
view of newspaper reports to the effect that the premier of British Columbia has rejected
the offer of financial co-operation with the government of British Columbia in the development of the Columbia river basin in Canada, would the Secretary of State for External Affairs care to comment on these newspaper reports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED REJECTION BY B.C. OF FINANCIAL CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
premier of British Columbia is quite a good horse trader. The statement, as reported in the Globe and Mail this morning, indicates that he is asking that the federal government take a second look at the problem. In addition, he has made some statements which are rather far of the mark.
For example, he is reported as saying that the federal government is trying to interfere in the development of British Columbia resources, and again that the federal government would be making a loan to the province of British Columbia.
The facts are that the federal government has offered to enter into a joint program with the province for the development of this self-liquidating project. This is the actual fact of the situation. Further, the federal government must make the treaty with the United States and, under that treaty, will be obliged to enter into a covenant to build various dams in British Columbia. This means that we shall be obliged to have an agreement between the federal government and the province of British Columbia which will bring about compliance with the terms of the treaty. In other words this is a three-party deal, with the federal government in the middle between the United States government and the province of British Columbia.
The Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture and, I believe, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources are in Victoria now negotiating with ministers from the British Columbia government. I have no doubt that all these different factors will be given consideration at this conference. The meetings commenced yesterday and they are continuing today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, December 7, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for the second reading of Bill No. C-49, respecting technical and vocational training assistance.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill before us today has been received, I am sure, with rather mixed feelings. Certainly I must confess that my own feelings on this bill are rather mixed. Basically and in general the bill is quite a good one, but I think one of the difficulties is that this bill has been very badly misrepresented both to the public and to this house.
While the bill is a good one basically, I believe this house and this country as a whole were expecting something quite different. We all know that for many, many months, and in fact over a period of two or three years, this government has refused or failed to admit that there was such a thing as an unemployment problem in this country. We are very happy to see that has changed and that the government has Anally admitted that there is such a problem. This is an improvement, and we are very glad to see it. But unfortunately there has been an attempt to pass off this bill as a solution to the unemployment problem that we face. I think we will And, on examination of this bill, that it is no such thing. I think this is rather unfortunate; I think it is unfair to the bill, it is unfair to the government and it is unfair to the people of Canada.
This bill is a step in the right direction In fact, Mr. Speaker, I might say that s good description of this bill is that it would be a good C.C.F. bill under normal conditions. But certainly it does not and cannot meet the emergency we have facing us at the

present time. I think the minister and the government realize this. I think this is an admission we find in this bill in clause 4, subparagraph (c), which refers to a 25 per cent bonus, in its aggregate, payment by the federal government which will apply:
-for the purpose of providing a technical and vocational training program for unemployed persons-
That is after March 31, 1963. This is a tacit admission by the government that it has no cure for this problem, that it expects it to continue; and that is why at this time the house is being asked to take action to prepare for the conditions we shall have to meet by 1963. I think this is a serious admission by the government.
On second reading we are dealing, of course, with the principle of the bill. I do not want to discuss the various clauses at this time, because I know there will be an occasion to do that later. However, before we can understand the principle of this bill I believe many explanations will have to be made with regard to these various clauses.
For example, in clause 3(l)(b) we find provision for training persons in regular secondary schools. One wonders just how this would be arranged. Is the federal government intending to enter this field, a field which I believe, comes entirely under provincial jurisdiction? Is it the intention now to pay subsidies toward the teaching of the regular school curriculum in the provinces? Some explanation is necessary before we should be asked to vote on the principle here.
Again, in subclause (c) reference is made to the training of persons as teachers, supervisors or administrators. How is that going to work out? Is it to be something additional to the present system, or something parallel with it? What are the government plans, or in other words what is the principle of this bill in this respect? Again, further on in the clause reference is made to supervisors in industry. Is this something new? Another item is to be found in subclause (h). where reference is made to disabled persons. Persons are disabled for various reasons, some as a result of accidents in industry in respect of which they receive workmen's compensation. Does this apply in the circumstances envisaged in the bill? As I say, I think there are many explanations which the minister should make with regard to all these matters before we are asked to pass this bill in principle.
To carry this a step further, I think some explanation should be given, in particular, with regard to clause 4 in which we find the aggregate of the various portions of the cost to be paid by the federal government. In clause 4(2)(a) there is reference to 50 per cent of the capital expenditure incurred by the
Vocational Training
province on training facilities, and the next subclause (b) refers to 25 per cent of the capital expenditure incurred by the province on training facilities before the 1st day of April, 1963. The following subclause goes a little further than that, and I should like to read what it says:
(c) twenty five per cent of the capital expenditure incurred by the province after the 31st day of March, 1963 for the alteration or repair of premises and the purchase of machinery and equipment, under circumstances specified in the agreement, where such alterations, repairs and purchases are for the purpose of providing a technical and vocational training program for unemployed persons.
Is this entirely different from the first two items? Is there, for example, to be assistance only for the purchase of machinery and equipment after 1963? If it is not different, why is it listed separately in the clause. Here again I think an explanation should be given by the minister. Otherwise this provision would really be meaningless, because it would certainly fall in the category of pie in the sky by and by.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that the hon. member is anticipating the debate which will be possible in the committee stage. The principle of the bill is a contribution to the cost of the various forms of technical and vocational education but the details, percentages and specific objectives are more properly discussed when they come before the committee, except in so far as general comparisons can be made and it is necessary to refer to details for that purpose. It seems to me the hon. member is getting into a rather detailed examination of the bill on second reading.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. When I started out I mentioned that I felt required to refer to specific clauses, hut only as they apply to the principle of the bill. We are now asked to pass a bill in principle. Before we can take an intelligent decision I think we must have some explanation of what are the principles involved in these various clauses.
If I may continue for a moment with regard to clause 8, I believe it introduces an entirely new principle in this country. This, of course, refers to technical training of members of the armed forces. Is the Minister of Labour going to take over this type of training? Is the government going to institute parallel training? I believe this is a vital factor in regard to the principle of the bill.
The next point I want to deal with is in my opinion the most serious of all. You have to be something of a bloodhound to trace it throughout the various twists and turns. I refer hon. members to page 3, subclause (b) (ii) of clause 3, referring to technical and

Vocational Training
vocational training programs of the type described in paragraphs (c) to (h) of subclause (1). Turning back to that reference in the bill we find that it refers to clause 8. Following that diligently through we find it refers to the training of any person serving in the naval, army or air forces of Canada.
In reading the balance of the clause we find the principle involved. Referring to the contributions payable it is provided that 100 per cent will be paid-we have always paid that amount-and then it goes on to say "or such lesser percentage thereof as may be specified in the agreement". That is certainly a brand new principle. It appears to be an attempt by the federal government to shove off on the provinces through various agreements that will be made the responsibility of technical training for our armed forces.
We have seen the Prime Minister trying to shove off on the provinces the responsibility for income tax. We cannot help wondering if this is part of an over-all pattern that is developing in the country.
I believe this is an important principle. On the face of it this appears to be an innocent clause, but my experience in dealing with agreements, contracts and negotiations suggests that the innocent clauses are the ones to which the most attention should be paid.
I believe there are three main weaknesses in this bill, the first of which was dealt with in part by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) when he spoke the day before yesterday. This bill, like so many others introduced by this government, unfortunately places the provinces in a position where those which need assistance most can afford it least; those which have the greatest need for this assistance are the ones least able to take advantage of it.
The second and I think the biggest weakness is that despite the search I have made of the bill from beginning to end there is no apparent provision for the families of the unemployed to enable them to take advantage of this training if and when it is set up. It is not enough to provide facilities. We have university facilities in this country today and have had for many years, but unfortunately not enough of our people are able to take advantage of them. According to the last figures I saw, seven people are going to university for every 1,000 pupils who started elementary school. It is not going to do much good to set up technical training schools across the country if we do not have the pupils to attend these schools. We solve nothing.
In my view this might be a good bill to prevent a crisis at some future date, but I

should like to reiterate that we have a crisis on our hands now and now is the time when we should be meeting it. This bill is certainly not the answer to meet the crisis at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on Bill No. C-49. I wish to congratulate the minister first on bringing in the bill because of the training that will be given many young people who otherwise would only swell the ranks of the unemployed and, second, for spearheading this movement and for the payment of 75 percent of the cost of training these young people. No one can argue against the bill in a country like Canada. As a matter of fact I am sure the minister must have been embarrassed over and over again as praise was heaped upon him for introducing the bill.
It has been stated that 40 per cent of our unemployed are under 24 years of age. This legislation will cut right into that age group of unemployed young people, many of whom are still capable of being trained and should still be in school. The bill will allow them to acquire the skills and training that they need in order to become usefully employed.
I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members a press release concerning a report by the Department of Labour which was issued after a recent meeting of the apprenticeship training advisory committee. The report emphasizes that there are not enough apprentices being trained at the present time to meet either normal losses in industry through retirement or to replace those who are upgraded and so on, let alone to provide for the future needs of this country.
I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker, to a firm that came to Midland in 1952, a firm that we are very proud to have in my riding of Simcoe East. I refer to the Ernest Leitz company. Guenther Leitz came to Canada, established the firm there and became its first president. Basically they wished to do lens grinding and manufacture cameras, and the firm looked forward to the time when they could manufacture nearly all the camera parts in Canada except very special parts. Primarily what they wanted to do was to train young Canadians to do the lens grinding so that after a period of time there would be six skilled Canadian workers to every skilled German. The remainder of the German employees would return to the parent firm in Germany.
I wish to quote from the article in Saturday Night of December 10, 1960, to show just how well the plan has worked out:
The scheme to train Canadian youngsters in this exacting but highly paid trade has failed miserably. According to Walter Kluck, who is in charge of sales and finance, the attitude of young Canadians is such that "they simply do not wish to spend

about three years of their time learning a highly skilled trade which would ultimately enable them to earn very good money. They started here with good intentions, high hopes, and ambition, but when summer came the lure of more pay for transient jobs took them away and the training was wasted."
It was not for want of courage and determination on the part of the German firm, nor from lack of co-operation from the Ontario department of labour which, as long ago as 1956, expressed great interest in what was happening in the Leitz firm and lent its support to the creation of a set of standards to govern the requirements in the province for skilled precision optical workers.
Guenther Leitz, the president of the Canadian firm, has said that "in Germany apprentices start at the age of 14 to learn a skilled trade, but the educational system in Canada precludes young people from starting to learn a trade until 16 or later, by which time they tend to be attracted by higher rates of pay elsewhere-which are immediate but not long term."
As a specific example of these youngsters, Walter Bauer quotes one young man who stayed with the company three years and had only six months to go to become a skilled precision worker but threw it up and left when he found that he was not making as much money as a man who had been with the firm for over twenty years.
The Leitz people, and many other firms, wish that the provincial and federal governments would really do something about apprenticeship instead of talking about it. Perhaps there should be a system, as there once was, whereby the trainee enters into a binding contract. After all, the company is teaching him skills which will be of great financial value to him all through his life. But no company has any such guarantee now . . .
I wanted to refer to that to suggest that perhaps we should change our educational system enough so that young people could start apprenticeship training at the age of 14. Perhaps some system should be worked out whereby, if they have not enough basic education at the age of 14, they could take not only their apprenticeship training but also some of their basic studies. There would have to be some changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act to meet these requirements. There would also have to be some exemptions under the income tax law.
Perhaps this might solve the problem, because there does not appear to be any great number in Canada who are qualifying through apprenticeship training. This is not a problem of today, Mr. Speaker. This condition has existed since long before 1950. Over the years we have been bringing skilled workers from Great Britain, Germany and other countries in Europe. If we had been watching we would have known that these fields were drying up. As we watched Germany become a great industrial giant again, and as we watched Great Britain and Europe rise from the ashes of decadence and destruction to the position they now occupy, we should have known that this situation would be facing us and we should have been training apprentices to do the necessary skilled work.
Vocational Training
In order to prove this statement I think all we have to do is look at the facts in the labour field. Of those who have not finished their primary education we find that 19 per cent are unemployed. We also find that 8 per cent of those who finished their primary education are unemployed, while in the case of those who completed their primary and secondary education the number of unemployed is just about one third that figure. I think that points out to us the necessity of seeing that our young people are educated. In my view the manufacturer should be protected to some extent by having the apprentice agree to finish his training, and in return the manufacturer would agree to give such training that when the young apprentice had finished he would have the necessary experience to engage in industry anywhere in Canada in whatever line he had been trained.
Surely the thinking that has built up over the years must be changed. The young people must be encouraged to enter those fields that will not only be very rewarding for them but also very productive for the state. This is a very necessary step for Canada to take. The old idea, as I have said, of importing key workers in an industry has now gone. The policy of the past government has dried up. There are no more key workers obtainable from industrial Germany and Europe. We have now approximately 250,000 young people coming into the labour market every year. These young people must be looked after. Our young people must be trained so they are equal to the best in the world. Nothing short of this is good enough. Canada must reach the heights and the destiny that the fathers of confederation predicted for her.

speechtext:
stand to support the principle of this bill. Bill No. C-49, which we have before us, is one of the measures introduced by the government to combat the economic emergency which we now have in this country. I say this because of the statement made by the Prime Minister in his broadcast of December 21, in which he said that the plans were already made and would be presented in detail at the next session of parliament. He was referring to unemployment. Naturally, he said, "I cannot say what those plans are in connection with those matters which will require the approval of parliament, but I can assure you they will be based on a current and realistic appraisal of the unemployment problem".
The Minister of Labour, in introducing the bill on technical vocational training said, as recorded on page 231 of Hansard for November 25, I960:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution introduces legislation to stimulate technical and vocational training and broaden its scope throughout Canada. It is designed to undergird the government's program to increase employment and foster national development.
I support the principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker, for a number of reasons; first, because it is a measure which in the long term will tend each year to eliminate one of the greatest causes of unemployment which we have in this country today. I support it, too, because I think it will broaden the educational service which is now being given to Canadian youth. I further support the measure because I think it will increase the number of trained personnel, whether the personnel concerned are employed or unemployed at the moment.
Plowever, sir, there are some considerations in connection with this bill about which I am not very clear, and I hope when we get to the committee stage the minister will be able to give us some clarification. I recognize, of course, that in talking about this particular type of bill we are probably not able to get all the answers we would like to have, for the simple reason that the arrangements which will be made by the provinces should be more properly discussed by the provincial governments than by the federal government. While those of us who have some idea as to what we would like to have in a technical and vocational scheme of education would like to have the thing spelled out in the bill, still I say it is more properly the concern of the provincial governments.
I think we have to face the fact that we do have in this country a changing pattern of unemployment. I think at the moment we have a hard core of unemployment that is not similar at all to the unemployment we have been accustomed to in years gone by.

Any attempt which is made by the government to ease the present unemployment problem must be based on the fact that the unemployment problem is a changing one.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that this is not only a problem for government but is also a problem for industry. I think it is a problem for the educational departments, and I certainly think it is a problem for the Canadian people as a whole. I say this problem is one that must be faced by a great many sectors of the Canadian population. I think it is the government's responsibility to give the proper lead in providing the services that are required. In these days we hear the statement that the cause of our unemployment is the fact that there are not enough jobs provided to meet the demand. I think there is a lot of truth in that statement, Mr. Speaker, but I also think the statement leaves a wrong impression in some instances, because it is my considered opinion that we not only have to provide more jobs for young Canadians but we have to change the nature of the demand.
Here, I think, is the importance of the measure before us. If we are going to allow young Canadians to enter the labour force and demand jobs that do not require skills, then we are allowing a type of labour force to be built up in this country which in the years ahead will be of great proportions. I say that while it is true we have to find more jobs for our Canadian people in order to meet the demand of labour, we also have to change the nature of the demand This, I think, is the importance of this bill. I hope that when the bill is implemented and the provinces have taken advantage of the provisions which are included in it, in the years that lie ahead we will be able to show that the demand for labour has changed and young Canadians are able to take advantage of the types of training that are being offered.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that in the long run automation will make fewer jobs in this country. In the short run that may be true, but I do believe that automation will make more jobs for those who are prepared to take them. If we are going to continue in the years ahead to have somewhere between 175,000 and 220,000 young people come out of our high schools and allow the majority of these students to be forced into the unskilled labour market, then I think we must also accept the fact we will have a large amount of continuing unemployment for some time.
I think we live in a country in which there has been a gradual transition to the manufacturing and industrial aspects of our economy. If this is true, as I think it is, then in order to have people take their places in that

type of employment they must be trained to do the jobs that are required to be done. Nature, of course, has decided that there are those who, in their educational endeavours, will go through high school and on to university. Nature has also decreed that there are those who will be obliged to make their living through their special ability to employ certain skills. But those skills must be trained, and I believe those skills can be trained under the type of bill we have before us today.
We must also face the fact that we are living at a time when it seems there is more production with the employment of fewer people than was the case a few years ago. I believe that is a result of the last recession. If we look back over some of the statistics for employment and production, I think we shall find that more production is taking place with the employment of fewer people. The manufacturing industry is an interesting case. The employment index for the manufacturing industries in 1953 was 113, based on the 1949 figure of 100. In June of 1960 the employment index for the manufacturing industries was 112.1. Here we see that the manufacturing industries now are employing fewer people than they employed in the year 1953. However, when we look at the index for manufacturing production, we find that in 1953 the index for production was 147.4, yet in June, 1960 it was 157.8. In other words we are today producing larger quantities of goods and are using fewer people than we used in 1953.
The reason for this situation may not be easy to find. I suggest that it may be owing to the fact that some manufacturing concerns are operating in a more efficient manner. Again, other manufacturers have employed all the devices of automation which they can use in their industrial plants. But whatever the reason, we must face the fact that an increase in production does not necessarily provide a proportionate increase in the number of people employed. I therefore think it is necessary to train young people not only to take their places in the industries we have at the moment but also to take their places in industries which may be developed in the years that lie immediately ahead.
We are going to have a tremendous increase in the labour force within the next five or ten years. The possibility of the Canadian economy employing those young people will depend largely on the skills they have to offer. We know that today too many of our young people are leaving school at too early an age. When the Minister of Labour was introducing the resolution he made some comments in this regard, and I thought he put his finger on the real nerve end of the problem. We have too many young people leaving school at too
Vocational Training
early an age, with too little formal education, and having nothing to offer an employer who is going to pay the monthly cheque.
Suppose a young lad comes out of school at grade VIII or grade IX, goes up to a prospective employer and asks for a job. The employer says, "Yes, I can give you a job", at $150, $200 or $250 a month, as the case may be, "but what have you to offer me in return?" I think this is the question that every young lad coming out of school and looking for a job must answer. He must be able to go to a prospective employer looking for a job and, in return for the renumeration which he is to receive, must be able to offer something to his employer. In this day and age I do not think he can offer to his employer the things which can be expected unless he has a good formal education and some training in the field in which he wants to work.
Possibly part of the reason some of our young people are leaving school too early is that our schools are not offering those subjects which are interesting to the pupils concerned. I have had some experience in this field. In a large high school in which I worked for a number of years, we had some students who left before graduation. We had other students who failed in the final examinations. One of the things that always bothered me was that I thought a large percentage of those students failed not because they did not have the ability to reach certain standards of training, but because the school failed to offer them training in the things they would like to do.
In saying that, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am not a proponent of progressive education. However, I believe that the schools of our country should offer to our boys and girls training in the fields in which they and their guidance counsellors feel they have some capability. I know that many young lads who fail in mathematics, for example, would have a great deal more interest in the subject if they were going to an institution where the importance of mathematics in relation to mechanics-if the young lad wishes to take mechanics-was demonstrated. If the relation between mathematics and mechanics was shown to the young lad and he had an opportunity to get some training in mechanics, I have no doubt in the world that he would be much more interested in mathematics.
I therefore say again, Mr. Speaker, that maybe one of the reasons many of our young people leave school too early is that our schools are not offering the type of training which these young lads would like to have. Others, of course, leave for much different reasons. I think maybe we have reached the time in this country when educational authorities should sit down together with

Vocational Training
parents and discuss this matter in a thorough manner. I might also say that I believe we have in this country a large number of people who, even after they have left school, still have a good deal of time to give to some extra training, for example to go to night classes or take advantage of whatever opportunities are available.
I was interested the other day in reading a little pamphlet put out by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. This is the issue of November, 1960. It gives a table showing the number of hours worked annually by workers in six different countries. This table was compiled by the international labour organization. It shows that in Switzerland the annual number of hours worked is 2,416 or, based on a 50-week year, 48.3 hours per week. In West Germany the figure is 2,296 hours or 49.5 hours per week. In Sweden the figure is 2,212 hours annually or 44.2 hours per week. In the United Kingdom the figure is 2,192 hours per year, with a weekly average of 43.8 hours. In the United States the figure is 1,984 hours per year, with a weekly average of 39.7 hours. In Canada the figure is 1,928 hours per year, or 38.6 hours per week.
The interesting thing here is that the average Canadian works almost 500 hours less annually than his counterpart in Sweden, or his weekly work time is short by from five to ten hours. I believe this is a good thing, Mr. Speaker. What I am trying to point out here is that since we are living in a country where a man is able to make a living by working a shorter number of hours every year, he has the time to partake of any extra educational services which may be offered to him. I believe we have many young men in this country who are employed today and who could profit greatly by being able to attend evening classes, technical school, vocational school, or even the regular classes, and improve their formal education.
I was also interested in the investigation that has been made in the other place. I refer particularly to a statement made by Mr. Denton, who was then before the committee of the other place. This is the statement which he made, as it is found on page 30 of the first report of the Senate committee on manpower and employment:
There is a strong relationship between education and unemployment. In February of this year the dominion bureau of statistics undertook a special survey of the educational attainments of persons without jobs in connection with its regular monthly sample survey of the labour force. The results were striking. The unemployment rates for people who did not complete primary school were more than twice the rates for people who completed primary school but did not complete secondary school, and six times the rates for people who completed secondary school. These results relate to a single survey at the seasonal

peak of unemployment, but there is every reason to believe that, broadly speaking, they represent a general situation, that although the rates vary from season to season and year to year, they are typically much higher among people with little education, and that the rates decline sharply as the number of years of schooling increases.
I believe this is a very significant statement. I think it is a statement that should be made all across this country so that employers, educational authorities and parents may give to it the really serious consideration it deserves. It has always been my opinion that the Canadian people have never spent enough money on education. These are days when we hear from cities, municipalities and all the provinces that they are unable to find the amount of money required to meet the educational demands being made on them. In the year 1959 Canada spent approximately $1J billion on education. This was 4.2 per cent of the gross national product.
When I was looking for some information to include in my remarks on this bill I tried to find the relation between the amount of money which Canada spends on education as compared to its gross national product, to compare it with the same figure for other countries. I was unable to obtain all the information that I had hoped for, but I would hope that the surveys which are now being made by the department and also the inquiry being made by a committee of the other place will make some effort to compare the amount of money being spent on education as compared with the gross national product in Canada, compared with similar figures for other countries.
While we spent $1J billion on education in Canada in the year 1959, a very small percentage of that was spent on technical education. Around $57 million was spent on technical education in Canada in 1959, or only 3.7 per cent of the total amount of money spent on education of all forms. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that we live in a country where I believe this amount is too small to produce the type of young Canadian this country is going to need within ten or fifteen years. I say this for the simple reason that we have a changing economy and we have, as I said before, a changing type of employment. There is something seriously wrong with this situation, and I believe it is the type of thing that is not going to melt away and is not going to be decreased unless it is attacked in a proper way with a proper knowledge of the problem.
In my own province we have been devoting a considerable proportion of the total expenditure of the provincial government to education. It has shown results. We have, too, a program for technical education which I hope will be able to show some real results

within the next few years. In my own home city of Corner Brook we have one of the finest apprenticeship programs in Canada in connection with the Bowater paper mills. I was in Corner Brook when this program was started some years ago. I have always had the greatest respect for it, and when I look now at the type of young man this scheme has been able to develop, I feel it has been most worth while. My only regret is that we have not been able to provide a similar service to a greater number of Newfoundlanders.
In my own home city, too, the association of university women is taking a real interest in technical and vocational education. Over the last year or two they have had a series of meetings in which they have tried to acquaint themselves very thoroughly with the problems of technical and vocational education. When they are in a position to make their report I think they will be able to make a substantial contribution to the thinking on technical and vocational education in Newfoundland.
Mr. Speaker, I believe one of the things we have to do here is build the type of building necessary for technical and vocational education. We have to produce the type of instructor who is well qualified, not only in terms of education but qualified also to be accepted by industry and by a number of professional institutes in Canada. We have to provide those courses in technical training which will engender public confidence in the scheme, because one of our difficulties with technical and vocational training in Canada is that somehow or other there is a feeling that this type of education is inferior to the type of education given, for example, in the professions.
I believe that if this problem is attacked in the proper way we can develop the proper attitude toward technical and vocational training. I think it is a problem that really needs some attention in this country today. Mention has been made during this debate of what is happening in Russia. We all agree that great advances are being made in Russian education along certain lines, but I would hope that a country like Canada would never be stampeded into developing a system of education that is loaded on the scientific side. I believe that a true system of education must be balanced to suit our needs at any one particular time. I think it should be flexible enough to produce the technologists and technicians that are required at any one time. But we must never lose sight of the fact that no democracy will ever be able to maintain itself without a true respect for the arts and humanities. I do
Vocational Training
hope that those who look at what is happening in Russia will never feel that we would sacrifice one side of the educational picture for the other.
On the other hand, we must face the fact that education must produce the trained personnel required. All hon. members will agree that one of the most important things about education is that it helps us to live our lives. It must also help us to make a living. I do not want to be irreverent when I say that one cannot live by bread alone. Nevertheless, it might well be remembered that bread is mentioned. While education helps us to live our life, it must also help us to make a living.
Finally, if we can take this theory of education and carry it to the Canadian people and get them to dignify technical and vocational training to the extent that they have dignified other types of education, then I think we shall have served the Canadian people well. There is one thing we must remember. Man is not only another link in the long chain of evolution; he is the very reason for its development.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Every parliament produces important legislation. Every session of every parliament produces

Vocational Training
important legislation. As one of those whose main role in this house is that of observer, may I say that in my humble opinion the legislation now before us is of paramount importance. This is because we are dealing here with human material; we are dealing with men, and perchance women, who in a few years will take over the leadership of industry, commerce, agriculture and government. I believe the government and the minister are to be sincerely commended for having introduced a bill of this type.
It is not my intention to repeat what has already been said in this house. The field has been very carefully covered. I should like to be specific with respect to one phase of vocational education, however, and the desire to do this was prompted in me the other day by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken), who in the course of a very thoughtful address containing a number of valuable suggestions drew a picture of the transition which had taken place among the population from farms to cities in the last few years. She quoted figures showing the drift of our people from the farms into the larger centres, and she had some very responsible and helpful comments to make with respect to them.
My main interest is in agriculture, as you know, Mr. Speaker, and I am concerned about this drift from the farms in western Canada. It is not my wish to be regional in any recommendation I may make, but we do have a situation in western Canada where our young people, along with their fathers and mothers, are leaving the farms and endeavouring to find employment In industry and commerce in the centres of the prairie provinces. Alongside this situation there is the development, by the inspiration of this government and by the activities of the provinces, in the field of irrigation. We are changing the type of agriculture in western Canada by the use of water from our snowshed on the east side of the Rockies, removing from agriculture the hazards that lie in the path of a dryland operator who may have experienced drought or who may have found his water supply totally insufficient for the successful production of livestock.
Thus when we get into this vocational training program I do think a great opportunity presents itself to train some of our young farm people, not for work in industry or elsewhere but for work in their own industry of agriculture. We could render a great service not only to them but also to the country. Hon. members may ask what specific action can be taken with respect to vocational training in irrigation. Let me say in answer to that question that any type of farming in Canada today is a highly technical operation. That is the case in Ontario, in Quebec, in

the maritimes or in western Canada. The operation of an irrigated farm is particularly technical because it requires a knowledge of survey and of water application as well as the intricacies of the machines which are used in this particular field of agriculture.
Here my mind goes back to the days of the dark thirties when there was a need for taking up the slack with respect to a great many young people who were unemployed, and as a result of the action of the government of that day in co-operation with the western provinces, youth training centres were established. I had the privilege in those days of playing a small part in connection with those schools. I can see today in my neighbourhood and in other neighbourhoods in the province of Alberta the far-reaching effect and value of those youth training centres. It may sound very casual when I say we taught them blacksmithing, carpentry and something about crop sequence and community life, but all these things go to make up the building of a country. Were it necessary I could quote chapter and verse to show where this councillor, this member of the legislature, this member of parliament, this leader is a product of a youth training centre in the province of Alberta during the thirties.
In the province of Saskatchewan we are spending a lot of money on the South Saskatchewan dam. We are pouring millions of dollars into irrigation developments in southern Alberta. Yet there is no centre in Canada where a young person having the desire to do so may go in order to become a skilled ir-rigationist. So I say to the minister that those who will have to formulate the actual plans as a result of this legislation can render a great service and be of great value not only to this generation but to the nation if they will take cognizance of the fact that this remarkable transformation of western agriculture as a result of these vast irrigation projects is worthy of some attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour, after listening to the comments from all sides of the house, must be getting a swelled head; because his greatest critic said nothing, in effect, but that this is a dandy bill which hon. members of his party would support. Then he introduced the usual "but" and brought out a few points that he would probably describe as criticism, differences of opinion, etc. Even the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) in his great tirade did not have too much criticism to offer, as you will see if you examine his speech closely.
However, there is another reason why the minister might well get a swelled head, and

that is because of the nature and quality of the speeches that have been made on all sides of the house. A fine example this morning was the speech made by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten). The hon. member made a factual speech, and a lot of work must have gone into its preparation. If anything, it bears out the need for a measure such as the bill presently before us. I liked the way the hon. member developed his speech and tied in all the ends. To those hon. members of the house who glance over Hansard occasionally I commend the reading of his speech.
It has been said before that Bill No. C-49 is designed to give a stimulus to technical and vocational training throughout Canada. The bill is another government measure brought forward during this session in an effort to combat unemployment. This is an effort in which we all must co-operate, but I would go a step further and say that we should get rid of the word "unemployment" and say instead that this is another measure introduced for the purposes of assisting employment in Canada. To my mind this is a much more constructive way of approaching the subject.
After examining the various measures that have come forward this session I am appreciative of the fact that the object of this bill is to look ahead and on a short term and long term basis combat the ever-growing unemployment situation. The fact that we have an unemployment problem today is not a situation unique to this government. We in Canada have had to face an unemployment problem throughout the years, and we will probably be faced with this problem in varying degrees for many years to come. It is something with which all have to grapple.
This bill seeks provincial co-operation and financially we are upping the ante, as it were, because the federal government is increasing its contribution, which is a welcome step. I do not want to go too much into detail in discussing the various aspects of the bill but will content myself with throwing out one thought which I believe has been expressed in one way or another by other hon. members who have spoken, principally by the hon. members for Simcoe East, York-Humber and one or two others. The idea I wish to contribute is that the whole country must train and develop itself in just a slightly different way in relation to the question of employment.
What I should like to see is an all out effort on a national scale to prove to all boys and girls, men and women, that it is a mistake to leave school unless it is absolutely necessary, and that to remain in
Vocational Training
school, on the other hand, is to provide for oneself a form of job insurance.
I am wondering if it would be difficult to sell this idea to all young Canadians. It certainly should not be. The problem has been aggravated by the fact that youngsters were able to leave school and take unskilled jobs at fairly good pay. Most of those who left school during the last five years felt they were launched on a career, but as we all know times have changed and there has been an altered picture in the manpower demand.
Look at the employment and unemployment figures. I believe they hold a rather grim lesson. All of us should study and examine these figures. Boys and girls in school and their parents should be aware of these figures from month to month and know exactly what they mean. I refer, of course, to the employment and unemployment figures supplied each month in Canada. The latest figures I have are for October, 1960 broken down into five-year age groups, as

It is interesting to note that there are only 560,000 employed in the 14-19 age group as compared with 1,441,000 employed in the 25-34 age group. The thing that strikes me about these figures is that there are more unemployed in the age group 14-19 than in any other five-year age group. When you consider the actual numbers who are employed in this group this is out of all proportion. I believe it points up a moral. If you have a trade and are a skilled worker there is not so much chance of your being unemployed. I wish to repeat that the best form of job insurance is education and we must sell this idea to our young people. Once this is accomplished we must make the means of education available to our young people, as this government is doing through the measure before us.
Various hon. members who have participated in this debate have suggested that this training should perhaps start at an earlier age, and I think I am in agreement with that idea. They have a fine educational system in England, where at the tender age of approximately 11 years the students are segregated according to ability. These are not hard and fast rulings and the system is flexible. A student who has been directed

Vocational Training
to vocational training will perhaps two years later show an aptitude for academic training and be redirected in that field. I believe it would be worthwhile to introduce a similar concept in the Canadian educational system.
Another point comes to my mind. The federal government will participate very heavily in the further education of unemployed persons. The age at which one may leave school varies from province to province; in some it is age 14 and in others age 16. It seems to me rather ridiculous that the federal government should pay for what in effect are unemployed children in the 14-16 age group when they should be in school and should not have left unless for a very valid reason. So far as those aged 14, 15 or 16 are concerned, might it not be a good idea for the government to step in and say, "All right, we will subsidize"-I hate to use the word "subsidize" but I suppose it is one way of putting my point across-"education at that level so that these young boys and girls, 14, 15 or 16, will not leave school but will receive further training, technical or otherwise". They would then remain in school and not enter the employment field until such time as they would have had further training in a skill and had become tradesmen of one sort or another.
With federal participation being boosted, I can see no reason at all why the provinces will not grab at this idea and go ahead with the building of more schools of the type required. In this regard I feel that in the province of British Columbia there is need to expand considerably and, coming from the Okanagan valley, I should like to see a technical or trade school constructed there. Where it should be located would be a matter for further study.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must be pleasant to the ears of the Minister of Labour to hear such complimentary remarks not only from his colleagues but from members of the opposition. I wish to join with those who have already spoken in complimenting the minister and the government on introducing this bill, because in my opinion it is a measure which is going to go a long way in solving some of the problems about which we are so concerned today.
Vocational Training
I take exception to the remarks made by some members of the opposition in which they tried to scare us by talking about a crisis now. The government realizes that whatever this bill is intended to do, it is not all going to be done now. It is going to be done within a few years. This government is not invading the field of education, which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. This government is prepared to subsidize and assist the provinces in establishing certain schools.
We have in the ranks of the unemployed young men and women who find it difficult to fit into any of the occupations or industries named in this bill. I refer to manufacturing, construction, commerce, fishing and agriculture. When a young man or woman completes high school in any of our provinces, he or she has an academic training which does not fit him or her for any of these jobs. These young people naturally are anxious to get into jobs where they can earn their own money, so they try to get positions in which they will not need to spend too much time learning how to operate, say, a lathe or some piece of machinery in a manufacturing establishment.
I am very pleased indeed, Mr. Speaker, to note that according to the interpretation section of this bill, it is intended to offer training facilities to men and women who intend to enter the field of agriculture. Coming from a farm constituency such as Marquette, I know from experience the difficulty my farmers have in obtaining farm labour-I am referring to those who can afford to hire farm labour-when springtime comes. They have approached the unemployment insurance offices in the province-the nearest one is at Brandon-but in spite of the fact that there will be a long list of unemployed who presumably have indicated by their applications that they are fit, ready and willing to take jobs, nobody comes out of this office to go on the farm. I personally know of half a dozen farmers near my town of Oakburn who complained about this as late as last July.
What is the reason, Mr. Speaker? Is it the wages the farmer is prepared to pay? No, I do not believe so. I believe the wages compare very well with the wages paid in other industries if you take into consideration the fact that board and lodging are included. The wages range anywhere from $150 to $175 per month for eight months of the year or until freeze up. The board supplied by our farm women, Mr. Speaker, compares with anything you can find in the city. They often mislay their can openers. When the farm table is laid for the family and the hired help, it is a sight to see. But in spite of that, sir,

Vocational Training
it is difficult to obtain farm labour. It is difficult to get young men who are without work to go out to the farm. Do you know why? I believe it is because they are afraid they are not capable of handling the farm machinery. Our agricultural industry has been mechanized to a great extent. Anyone operating farm implements must know how to use them, how to take care of them and how to take care of himself when he is using them.
Gone are the good old days. In the pioneer days when my father came out to this country, the farmer who hired him gave him an axe. The farmer cut one tree to show him how it was done, and my father learned that job right away. Anyone who came out to work for a farmer and was expected to milk cows was shown where he could pick up the stool and under which part of the cow he should sit. He was shown the four parts of the cow that provided the milk, shown how to squeeze, and the job was learned. It takes more than that to learn how to operate a milking machine, how to keep it clean and how to repair it if it does not run. It took no mental exertion or time to learn to harness a team of oxen. It did not take long to teach your hired man how to currycomb an outfit of horses, usually four. You had to get up at five o'clock in the morning to currycomb the horses, harness them, feed them and hook them on to a gang plow. It did not take long to show how to adjust a plow and raise the coulter, how to deepen the cut or how to get off in time if you happened to approach a stone. The same conditions applied to a seed drill or a simple binder drawn by oxen or horses. These things did not take long to learn. The most complicated part was threading the twine into the needle in case the threader lost the twine and that was easy.
Today, Mr. Speaker, the farm labourer is expected to know more than that. Any farmer who can afford to hire farm help cannot afford the time to teach the farm help. The farm labourer must know how to operate a tractor, and we have many different makes of tractors today. We have diesel tractors and gas tractors, and the farm labourer must know how to operate them and service them, as well as make minor adjustments instead of waiting for the farmer to come or running back to the farmhouse two or three miles away to get help. The farm labourer must be familiar with the bulldozer. The farm labourer must be familiar with the combine, which is an extremely complicated piece of machinery which cuts and threshes the grain. The farm labourer must be familiar with the farm truck. There is more to looking after a farm truck than there is to operating

an ordinary automobile. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the farm labourer must be capable of operating electric tools in order to make temporary repairs when necessary. But above all he must be familiar enough with the machines to be able to take care of himself. There is danger to life and limb in almost every piece of machinery the farmer uses today.
I have not the slightest doubt, Mr. Speaker, that every one of us could learn to operate the old horse-drawn machines. Those of us who do not know how to operate the old horse-drawn or ox-drawn machines could learn to operate them in half a day. However, I greatly doubt that many of us who are not familiar with the farm machinery of today could learn to operate it in a month. What farmer wants to hire help he cannot trust with expensive farm machinery such as the tractor worth $7,000 or $8,000 or the $8,000 combine? What young man wishes to go on a farm when all this machinery is not familiar to him? He is afraid. I have said that the farmer has no time to teach a novice how to carry out his duties if he hires him.
There is another aspect of the matter. We want young men on the farm. We want young men who will start farming. They may be sons of teachers, ministers or small town merchants. They are not like the boys who were born on the farm and grew up there, and who served their apprenticeship with their fathers. How do we expect them to go into farming? No matter what inducement you offer them by way of loans or by way of extended credit, or even if they are financially able to start farming on their own, they are afraid to go through their apprenticeship on their own expensive machinery.
I personally know of young men in my constituency who love the soil and would love to go farming. What do they do? They find that agriculture is an unknown field to them. They find them barging into the cities and swelling the ranks of the unemployed; or if they get a job, they are hooked on to the dinner pail for life.
I am pleased to note that agriculture has been given some priority in this bill. It has been placed first in the interpretation section. As I have mentioned before, this government, including the Minister of Labour, hopes that the provinces will co-operate. I believe the provinces have a duty to help to solve the difficulties. I hope the whole ten provinces will take advantage of this wonderful opportunity to establish technical and vocational schools. I hope my native province of Manitoba, which I am proud to say is under an extremely progressive Conservative government-will take advantage of the opportunities afforded and will teach our young

men what a tractor is, what it is made up of, what makes it tick and how it should be serviced, and will give the same instruction about the combine, the swather, the milking machine, the bulldozer and every bit of machinery that is used on the farm. If they were armed with that knowledge I am satisfied there would be hundreds and hundreds of men who would be prepared to take farm employment. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that my farmers would be glad to pay good wages to men upon whom they could rely to look after that machinery, who would know how to operate it and how to take care of themselves.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the house took recess.
