subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to join with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) in saying just how much I feel this bill could do for agriculture and for those who are interested in joining that industry. I think the hon. member has performed a very excellent job in explaining the tremendous advances in methods of farming in this country. I am sure the farmers in my constituency will be very pleased with the attitude taken by this government in trying to promote the interest of young men in that industry.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak on a somewhat different aspect of this bill, in the main as it refers to the retraining of persons in new vocations. Coming from Nova Scotia I know the difficulties with which people are confronted when they find themselves unemployed through no fault of their own and their vocation destroyed.
It is a sad day in a man's life when he learns that the vocation in which he has been trained and in which he has spent the greater part of his life is no longer one in which he can usefully be employed. In this realistic legislation the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr)

Vocational Training
is trying to replace the frustration of this situation with hope for the future, and he is deserving of great praise for his efforts in this regard. Coming, as I do, from Nova Scotia and representing the constituency of Cumberland I am well aware of the frustration which many in my province have faced and are continuing to face in connection with this problem.
In the town of Springhill as a result of two tragic disasters in 1956 and 1958, the citizens saw the industry disappear upon which they had depended for generations, and with it the need for their highly skilled vocation. It is difficult for a person to comprehend just what happens to an individual when his life long vocation is taken from him and he is left in the later years of his life with nothing he can do except ordinary unskilled jobs.
There are two things that a highly skilled vocation gives to an individual. One is creative ability, together with an interest and pride in the work done, and the other is a higher standard of living than he could expect to obtain in a semi-skilled or unskilled position. Many of the people in my constituency have had to forego a relatively high standard of living in exchange for a standard of living at subsistence level. I do not think that I, personally, am able to appreciate just how difficult it must be to face such a situation. Certainly it is a great shock, especially to persons in the later years of their lives, to have to make these difficult changes.
It is not only the people of my constituency who have had to face these difficulties. In Pictou county this situation occurred at an earlier date and today all Nova Scotians are anxiously watching developments in connection with the proposed closure of mines in the area of Cape Breton which will produce the same unhappy results.
In this country of ours today we cannot afford the luxury of destroying the vocation of an individual without providing a suitable alternative in order to retain that individual as a contributing force in our society. In Springhill I have watched highly skilled miners who have given the best years of their lives to this vocation, and who have made a tremendous contribution to the overall stability of my constituency, become not only unemployed but, worse still, unemployable because of the lack of a suitable program which would allow them to be retrained and, thereby, to continue to be an asset to society. Today the demand is for highly educated and highly skilled personnel. If a person has either of these qualifications he is in demand no matter what age group he finds himself in, but a man who is highly skilled in a vocation which is no longer in demand finds

that his chances of employment are slim if he is over 40 years of age, while if he is over 50 years of age his chances of employment are almost negligible.
The situation in Springhill is still capable of solution if the unemployed are provided with an opportunity for retraining; retaining not just in a vocation which might provide an opening but in one for which the individual appears suited. Individuals applying for vocational training should be carefully screened to determine their aptitude for the positions available, thereby eliminating as far as possible any failures that might result after training. I have talked with a great many people in my constituency who have come to me on different occasions, and said, for instance, that they would like to receive training as meat cutters, or carpenters or plumbers. I do what I can for them and telephone the individual in charge of placing these people in vocational training schools. But I am told, for instance: Sorry, but we do not have an opening for a meat cutter or a carpenter; however, we have one here for a cook; do you suppose this man would be interested in taking a course in cooking?
There is not much sense in trying to train a person in a vocation for which he has no aptitude, but I am afraid that is often the case today. There are not enough schools available and, as a result, there are not enough courses to make it possible for people to take the courses in which they are interested. We must try, in co-operation with the provinces, to provide a wide variety of courses and as many facilities as possible in order that the people who wish to be trained or retrained may have an opportunity to receive instruction in the course for which they have an aptitude.
Further, we must expect and, indeed, demand, the full co-operation of industry in this program. Without this co-operation we will not be able to secure the on the job training which the individual needs after he has finished his training course. If industry does co-operate, as I am sure it will, this program can be a tremendous success. There is no greater crime than that of throwing men out of work and out of a vocation to which they have contributed the best years of their lives,	without providing some alternative means	by	which they	can	continueto contribute	to	their areas	and	to theircountry. This	bill	appears to	have	the key
which, if used to its fullest degree, can open many doors for the people of my province.
This measure provides for more generous assistance to the provinces in the establishment of vocational and technical schools. With respect to unemployed persons the contribution can be as much as 75 per cent of

the cost of the program, and for veterans as much as 100 per cent. In addition, there is a contribution by the federal government of 75 per cent of the cost of the capital expenditure incurred by the province in the training facilities up to 1963, and 50 per cent after that date. In the light of the more generous assistance now available the provinces will no doubt be very willing to undertake a more concentrated attack on our unemployment problem especially as it applies to the semiskilled and unskilled workers.
As the result of the technological advances which have taken place there has been a marked change in the demands on our labour force. Employment has shown a marked increase in the professional and skilled categories with a much smaller increase apparent in the unskilled categories. If we are to accept the benefits of technological advances we must at the same time accept the responsibilities that are associated with them. This bill provides the means to do just that and it is my hope the opportunities inherent in it will be seized upon at the earliest possible date.
There is one area that is deserving of further consideration. Where a man is unemployed or employed in an unskilled or semi-skilled vocation and wishes to obtain the necessary training that will place him in a skilled category it should be available to him. Many today would like to obtain training but are held back through financial obligations to their families. If we are to have an effective program we must provide the means whereby a person can obtain this training and have a sufficient income available to him during the training period to allow himself and his family to survive what in many instances might be a very difficult period. It is my understanding that limited funds are now available to persons on these courses, enough to allow a single person to exist during the period in question but if we are to accomplish the retraining of persons of the type that find it a necessity in my constituency we must develop the system of assistance still further.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this occasion I must first congratulate the minister and the government upon bringing forward this legislation which I feel will provide the necessary incentive in my area for the construction of a long sought after vocational school. For quite a number of years the people of my constituency have required a school of this nature not only to alleviate the unemployment problem but to help meet the problem faced by workers in all parts of the country whose lack of skill and training precludes their taking part in the general expansion of the Canadian economy.
Vocational Training
It has been brought out by previous speakers in this debate that over 60 per cent of the unemployed in Canada today have grade VIII or less in the way of formal education and this is proving to be a great detriment in their seeking work in various fields. I do not wish to repeat what has been said by those who have already participated in the debate. However, I should like to commend some of those who have spoken for the constructive approach they adopted in relation to this bill. The negative approach adopted by some hon. members of the opposition leads me to wonder just what their purpose is.
The main feature of the bill is to make provision for a 75 per cent federal contribution to new schools up to March 31, 1963. The intention here is to provide an incentive for the undertaking of such work immediately. It is perhaps not too optimistic to anticipate that this provision will result in a 50 per cent increase in the present facilities. It is here that I feel the measure will be most effective in the communities adjacent to my riding. Attempts have been made there to meet the problem but the financial difficulties faced by the municipalities have been considerable. As a result of the announcement of further assistance it will perhaps be possible for the city of Sydney to undertake construction of a vocational school. The city has said that if necessary it would undertake the building of the school and I am sure the legislation now before us will be a determining factor in making possible the construction of a school in that area.
The federal government will pay half the cost of operating technical schools and will pay half the cost of training technical teachers. Anyone who has carefully studied the bill will have to admit that it is the most positive step forward in the training field ever taken in this country. It will go a long way toward increasing the supply of skilled workers in Canada and by that very fact will make it easier for such people to obtain employment.
The report of the committee of the other house on manpower indicates that lack of training is one of the primary reasons why people are without employment in Canada today. There is a diminishing place in industry at present for those who lack training in the skilled crafts which are so necessary for the working force to provide itself with the deserved standards of living worthy of the working people. This bill will go a long way toward making up that deficiency.
I listened with great interest the other day -as I always do-to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). I would suggest that instead of coming into the house and

Vocational Training
making that kind of negative speech on every occasion the hon. member should make a recording and simply play it back. One advantage would be the time the house would save. Surely when the government brings in a measure as constructive as this which surpasses anything previously done in this field the least that could be expected from hon. members of the opposition would be support which would stress the positive aspects of the measure.
I fail to understand the attitude of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), as exemplified in his remarks as reported at page 599 of Hansard of December 7 as follows:
We are just pointing out how inadequate it is, how inept it is, how useless it is, and how much it lacks.
The hon. member, of course, was referring to the measure before us. Perhaps I may be forgiven for my failure to understand why hon. members of the opposition would vote in favour of such a bill after making such comments about it. It represents a most confusing approach to the whole matter.
I know that this bill will be very welcome in the maritime provinces. I am sure the provincial authorities will do everything they can to co-operate as they did in the past under arrangements not nearly as favourable as these. One of the first effects will be that shelved plans for the future construction of new training schools will be now taken off the shelf and implemented through taking advantage of the incentive provision. In this connection I should like to quote from an editorial in this morning's Globe and Mail, as follows:
The scheme outlined by Mr. Starr tackles two national problems at once. One problem is the shortage of skilled workers which has been with us for an entire generation and-as business and industrial executives are well aware-remains very much with us today. The other problem is the surplus of unskilled workers which has been with us-in the form of large scale unemployment-off and on for the last ten years.
There is no doubt that this bill will hit at both these problems simultaneously and in a more effective way than has been previously attempted.
All hon. members are reminded of this problem each and every day when the circulars from the civil service commission reach our desks advertising positions in the service. I find it most discouraging to read these circulars advertising positions which I realize cannot in any way be helpful to the unemployed persons in my constituency. These circulars advertise technical jobs and jobs which could be filled by students with a high school education. I suggest to the minister that these circulars would be more effective if they were directed to the high schools of this country.

I try at all times to bring this to the attention of high school students who unfortunately are not in a position to look forward to university education with the hope that they will recognize here a field in which they can train themselves for a very adequate position in life without the necessity of having university training. I humbly offer the suggestion that possibly these circulars could be directed to the high schools in order, as I say, that pupils who cannot look forward to formal university education will realize that here is an opportunity that only requires some initiative on their part and some further study to qualify themselves for positions that may be advertised.
I should like to quote briefly from the report of the committee of the other place on manpower. It has this to say:
There is a strong relationship between education and employment. In February of this year the dominion bureau of statistics undertook a special survey of the educational attainments of persons without jobs in connection with its regular monthly survey of the labour force. The results were striking. The unemployment rates for people who did not complete primary school were more than twice the rates for people who completed primary school but did not complete secondary school and six times the rate for people who completed secondary school.
This again emphasizes the remarks I have just made in respect of positions advertised daily by the civil service commission of Canada which does make opportunities available to students with at least high school training. The hard fact which is staring us in the face today, Mr. Speaker, is that in order to maintain security of employment in industry we must have skill and we must have training. It is this situation which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the government are trying to deal with by bringing down this bill. In the face of a bill of this scope and showing the imagination and logic which it does in coming to grips with the problem one wonders what the opposition hopes to accomplish by its constant negative attitude.
We in the maritimes have a great respect for education, so much so that it has often been said that our chief export is brains. I might point out that day to day this has become more apparent to me when I review the list of appointments to high office throughout the country and in government circles and note the appointment of more and more maritimers. As far as my own province of Nova Scotia is concerned, the list of appointments of people from that province to high government posts is an outstanding one.
In looking for some solution to the problem the former Liberal government set up a royal

commission some years ago and its only suggestion in this regard was a one-way ticket out of the maritimes. The bill before us today provides the possibility of not requiring such one-way tickets but of providing necessary and most essential skilled training to workers who, by reason of automation or technological change of some kind, find themselves without work. It is most necessary that steps be taken in this direction to deal with the problem and not follow the recommendation of the royal commission report that the people of the maritimes be given one-way tickets out of that area.
In the United States presidential campaign recently there was a lot of talk about a new frontier. The frontier of the future in this country, Mr. Speaker, is the frontier of education. Too much emphasis cannot be placed upon the merits of the bill now before us. Everybody realizes, of course, that education is a provincial matter but where automation is having such a direct effect on the working force of the country education is everybody's business. This does not mean that there cannot be areas of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. I say that these areas have been too much neglected in the past and I say that the people of Canada have suffered as the result of this neglect. The time has now come to repair that neglect. The time has come to broaden the frontiers of knowledge in this country.
In the way in which we in this country tackle that problem and resolve the problem of more education for our people, of increased technical skills and increased skills of every sort, there will lie the future progress of this country. The report of the committee of the other place has shown the need. It has shown that many thousands of Canadians do not have the skill, the education or the training necessary to hold a job in industry today.
There is a great gap somewhere in our system of constitutional responsibility. That gap must be closed. It can be closed by a joint effort on the part of the federal and provincial governments. This bill provides the means by which the gap can be closed. It provides an opportunity for Canadians to acquire the necessary degree of skill and training necessary at the present time. The problem before us is a very serious one. It will not be solved by the faint-hearted approach we have heard put forward by members on the opposition side. It will be solved by joint action and the bill provides for such action.
Before resuming my seat, I should once again like to thank the minister and the government for the opportunity which this legislation will provide, in my own constituency particularly, to initiate the necessary action to bring about in the very near future
Vocational Training
the much sought after vocational training system which for the past number of years has been to the forefront of local problems. It will provide the municipalities, as I mentioned before, with the opportunity to be able to meet their share of the cost. Despite what the hon. member for Essex East may have to say about the city of Sydney and its rundown condition, it is enjoying a high level of employment and everybody appreciates very much the announcement by the city that it is willing to assume the whole responsibility of building a school in order that unemployed workers and workers generally will have the opportunity of availing themselves of such training as will add to their skill and provide them with a much better chance to have a decent standard of living in the very competitive field of industry and business today.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put for second reading of the bill I should like to join with other members of the house in speaking about the problem of vocational training and more especially as it applies to the unemployed section of our labour force. The emphasis on vocational training, as has been pointed out, points to a great need in the changing picture of the Canadian economy and that need is to utilize properly the skill, knowledge and know-how of our young people.
In introducing the resolution the minister said that 15 per cent of the work force unemployed are unskilled. I would hazard a guess that of the 15 per cent a very small portion could be classed as high school graduates, and I should like to speak for a minute on the question of high school graduates and the opportunities that are afforded in our economy to absorb the thousands of young men and women who every day and every year are entering into the work force of the country upon graduation from high school.
What do we have to offer these young boys and girls today? The day of the apprentice system in this country is gone. A young man used to sign himself up with a tradesman, work for a period of say five years, and upon completion of his period of training he would be qualified in that particular trade. This was a good system for that time, but time marches on. The economy is such today that this apprentice system is no longer adaptable to our society. We must, therefore, look for a new means of providing people with the necessary skills to do these jobs. In my opinion, that is the merit in this legislation. Earlier in this year, I believe, the minister announced that the federal share of the cost of vocational training was to be

Vocational Training
increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent. This bill that is now before the house is an enlargement of that policy of increasing the federal cost of participating in vocational training.
I should like to give to the house an illustration of the problems connected with providing jobs and, more particularly, the training of people so that they may acquire the skills to fill the jobs. In my part of the country we have one of the oldest, if not the oldest, iron ore mines in Canada. Over the years a relatively large population has been built up around this single industry, until today there are about 14,000 people in this small mining town. Obviously this mine has not increased in size or scope to enable it to absorb the increase in the working force resulting from this increased population. The men who have worked in the mine all their lives and who, perhaps, have hoped to see their sons follow them, are now finding it necessary to break up their families and send them away to find new jobs.
In addition to that, the operations at this particular mine were cut back considerably more than a year ago. Incidentally, this mine is part of the Dosco empire, and when it was taken over by the A. V. Roe interests one of the three working mines was closed down, thereby adding to the list of unemployed by some 600. However, to illustrate the changing scene in our mining and other industries, I may say that at about the same time new mining industries were opening up in the north, particularly in northern Quebec and Labrador. One would naturally think that the people who were let out when this mine was closed would find work in these new mines. However, what do we find? We find that these mines employ different methods of operation which make it virtually impossible for these miners who were laid off from the Dosco mine to acquire a job. Applicants for employment were obliged to write an aptitude test which was designed specifically to determine whether or not a man had certain mechanical aptitudes adaptable to the modern, heavy mechanized equipment used by these mines. Consequently, these men did not qualify. Here is where this bill could be put to work, and could be put to work immediately.
As another hon. member pointed out during the early stages of this debate, I believe one of the real difficulties connected with legislation of this type which deals with education is the fact that you have 10 systems of education in Canada by virtue of the fact that, under our constitution, education is within the sovereign rights of the provinces. I think the real problem in taking this very useful

and very commendable step is the necessity for making the legislation adaptable, in the best possible way, to these various provincial systems of education. It would seem, in order to do this in the best possible way, that it is going to require the officials of the minister's department sitting down with the officials of the various provincial departments of education to ensure that the provinces are utilizing this measure to the fullest degree.
I feel that perhaps a start could be made in this direction with the high schools. I do not believe it is enough to provide vocational training for students who have left high school or who are not going to finish high school. You have, first of all, to start in the school itself. This could be done by the adoption of a standard aptitude test which would be applicable right across the country and which every provincial department of education would make a part of the regular curriculum. In my opinion, these tests should be given in the high schools in order to determine the type of trade or occupation to which a student is best suited. The application of these aptitude tests, which are now such a common part of modern industrial policies, will require certain highly trained teachers.
As I say, this points up one of the real problems in Canada today, the problem of the student who does not have the means, either mentally or financially, to go to a university. Too often we see these young men wasting some of the most productive hours of their lives standing on street corners, frequenting pool halls and so forth. These are the people to whom we have to adapt this legislation more specifically because, after all, they are the Canadians of the future. These are the men upon whom the industry of this country will have to depend in future years. I feel great emphasis should be placed upon this aspect.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the minister if, in his reply, he would cover some of the points I raised, particularly with regard to the application of an aptitude test. I should like to know whether it is the intention of the Department of Labour to correspond with the various provincial ministers of education to ascertain if some standard aptitude test could be applied? As someone once said, to work is to be happy, and we have taken on the responsibility, under this bill, of equipping our young people with the means of finding work so that they can form a productive and useful part of our society.

speechtext:
should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, on this bill dealing with vocational training for

agriculture. We have coming in the province of Saskatchewan a great change-over from dry land farming to irrigation. My first experience with irrigation was in taking trips, as we did in training and in teaching our farmers in central Saskatchewan or by making tours into southern Alberta. These trips relating to irrigation in Canada were to the Cardson-Magrath-Lethbridge area of sunny Alberta, the location of the first irrigation company in Canada established by the early Mormon settlement. I have made nine trips into this area in order to educate our people in central Saskatchewan in connection with what is to become a reality when the south Saskatchewan river dam is completed.
We found that through lack of vocational training and the lack of knowledge the changeover from dry land farming to irrigation is a great transformation and one needing a great deal of training. In the study we found that it took three generations to make irrigation a success in that area and the people still have their troubles through lack of knowledge and proper management. We found that through lack of proper management some of their problems have been caused by putting too much water on the land, thus spoiling the land for many years. The land must be seeded back to pasture and grass in order to bring it back into production. Our Alberta friends still have their problems particularly relating to capital work and soil management as well as research problems related to suitable crops and Canadian markets.
To summarize, may I say that my experience as related to irrigation problems not only applies to water on the land but to markets and crops and the problems encountered there. In conclusion may I say this. We must have proper research and we must point out most emphatically the need for intensive research and training.
In central Saskatchewan we are about to make that big change-over from dry land farming to irrigation. We can go back to the hungry thirties when our country was blowing away because of lack of knowledge in our farming operations and also, of course, through nature, with the drought and the high winds.
I should like to refer now to the beautiful country at Conquest in the centre of the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar. Conquest is on a level plain right on the open prairie, with not a tree in sight. During the hungry thirties that country was blowing away until we were down where we could see the plough creases in the soil. One man one night thought of a scheme of planting hedges. He planted a hedge around his section and at every 100 acres he planted another hedge 90205-6-43
Vocational Training
north and south. It was not long before the people saw the benefit. Today the beautiful country around Conquest can boast of 1,000 miles of hedges. Through a vocational training plan like this one, this work could have been done years ago.
A great tree planting program is going on all through my area at the present time. It not only beautifies the country but it also holds the snow in winter and troubles on the roads are reduced. It holds the snow on the land for much needed moisture in the summer and protects the land against blowing. I am just bringing this matter to your attention, Mr. Speaker, in order to point out that if we had had these programs in effect years ago the people of central Saskatchewan would have been saved a great deal of trouble.
As I say, we are changing over now from dry land farming to irrigation. We are going to benefit much from the experience gained by our Alberta friends. However, there is still a great field to be opened up in training the people for this great change-over which will be coming in a few years when the South Saskatchewan river dam is completed. There is the matter of the handling of water and what we shall be obliged to learn through experience. With this training, the change-over will come about much faster.
We have markets to figure out when we change over from wheat to the cattle industry. In time there may be such things as sugar beets and canning crops to which we shall be obliged to change over from wheat farming. This is going to take a great deal of training. I just wanted to say a few words on this bill and to indicate that it will benefit the farmers of central Saskatchewan in the training that it will make available for this great change-over which I am sure is going to come within the next 15 years or 20 years.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this government has realized that the need for all types of vocational training schools is at hand. The time is opportune for a school of vocational training as related to irrigation in the Rosetown-Biggar constituency.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO PROVINCIAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
In closing the debate on the second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of observations I wish to make on the statements that have been made by those participating in this debate. In listening to the speeches made it seemed to me that they could be divided into three categories.

Vocational Training
The first category was the one that I think merits commendation. They were observations of the constructive type in respect of this bill, and some suggestions were also made in those speeches. Then there were a couple of contributions that bordered on the nonsensical. To them I will not make any reference at this time. Then there were a couple that were almost in the realm of the fantastic and later on I should like to deal with some of the aspects of the contributions of that type.
However, to all hon. members of this house I wish to state this in response to the questions posed in respect of the categories that will be included in the training under this bill. I wish to state that this bill includes all training of all sorts and types below the university level. As to all training in that respect by the provincial governments this bill gives to the federal government authority for its full participation.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) asked about vocational guidance. I wish to say to him that vocational guidance has always been included as an integral part of the training program and it will be included as part of the costs shareable under the agreements with the provinces.
I want to point out that this bill provides for a program of education that could be categorized as a co-operative program with the provinces. It is designed for the immediate present. That is why we have the construction of these schools terminating on March 31, 1963 for participation to the extent of 75 per cent by the federal government in the expenditures made by the provinces. It is also designed for the future.
I feel that now is the time for us to start building for the future education of the people of this country in the training of Canadians to fit themselves into the labour force and gainful employment. This bill is designed for now and for the future. There should be a continuity in respect of this type of training at all times.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) as usual gave a constructive contribution to this very important subject. He did say that of course this is not the complete solution of unemployment. It is not the complete solution. This is one of the measures to deal with this problem that is facing us today and will be facing us in the future.
I want to point out that of course education comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces and the federal government can only extend it in centres, with the co-operation of the provinces, in order to tackle this problem in a more effective way. This is what this bill provides in the provinces. However, only time will tell whether this program has

been successful, and the success of the program rests upon the co-operation of the provinces with the federal government.
I now wish to deal with the contribution made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). I did mention that in my eight years in this House of Commons I have never heard such a speech. I am sorry the hon. member is not here. He called this bill a fantastic piece of legislation; he said it was a colossal failure; in other words, the bill was just simply no good. He also said that 15 per cent of our unemployed were unskilled. Actually what I did say, Mr. Speaker, was that the rate of unemployment amongst unskilled workers was almost 15 per cent, which is entirely different to what the hon. member said. Then he said that 15 per cent of the unemployed at the moment amounts to about 600,000. By rapid calculation, when you multiply that it comes to about 3,400,000, and that is practically half our labour force. So here was some fantastic phraseology by the hon. member for Cartier. He gave me the impression that his contribution was due to his complete ignorance of the operation of technical and vocational training in the past, present, or as proposed in this bill.
I want to deal with some of the matters covered by this bill. Training is provided free at vocational schools. The training of unemployed persons, of disabled persons and training in the primary industries-and that includes the agricultural industry-is provided free, without cost to the trainees, in all provinces. Living allowances are also provided to enable trainees to attend these centres. Transportation is also provided to the training centres, and home again. All these things are provided in this program.
The hon. member for Cartier read from the report of the vocational training branch, and I might say he made no attempt to read it correctly. He mentioned a few groups for whom training was provided and completely ignored the larger groups that were reported. He made the statement that only 8,000 persons received vocational training in trades. I submit that this displays a complete lack of contact with reality. If the hon. member for Cartier was at all conscious of what is going on in his own province he would know that vocational training is provided to over 100,000 people per year and the volume of training is proportional in other parts of Canada.
In the report of the labour department which the hon. member read I am sure he could plainly see that the report only sets out the enrolments in specialized programs that were given assistance. The total enrolment in technical and vocational training day and evening classes, as reported by the dominion bureau of statistics, numbered some

338,000 in 1938 and 1939. Also, according to the dominion bureau of statistics estimates, there has been a 16 per cent increase since that time.
I think the hon. member failed to understand that the proposed contributions to capital expenditures are not limited by a quota allotment, as all previous capital assistance in this field has been. The only limit is the amount voted by parliament. I submit that this is completely new.
The hon. member also suggested that if the government would subsidize trade schools and provide assistance to students it would be a step in the right direction. That is exactly what the bill does, only it goes much further; it provides for a contribution of 50 per cent of the cost of provincial trade schools. And it does not stop there. It also provides for a 50 per cent contribution of the operating costs of technical and vocational institutes and institutes of technology where our technicians are trained. It also provides for sharing equally with the provinces in financial assistance to students attending these institutes of technology.
In fact, this bill provides a 50 per cent contribution of the provincial training costs of all persons who have left a regular school system either before or after completing their education, and 75 per cent of the cost of training unemployed persons.
I am very pleased that the hon. members who have spoken on this bill have recognized the importance of another new feature of this legislation which will contribute 50 per cent of the cost of the professional training of technical and vocational teachers, as well as financial assistance which may be provided to them while in training.
The hon. member for Cartier said that another advisory council was being established. I say that is completely erroneous. This bill provides for an enlarged representation on the vocational training advisory council, and that is all. He also ridiculed the fact that this council met only twice a year. He failed to recognize that this is only an advisory council of this program and it is not an administrative council. It is free to call meetings whenever it wishes, at the call of its chairman. If meetings are held only twice a year, then that is certainly a decision of the council. If it feels more meetings are necessary in order to review the situation, it is free to meet more often.
Mr. Speaker, I think this is a good bill. It is designed to provide, on the long term basis, facilities and the necessary training for these people, with the co-operation of the provinces-which in the first instance must take 90205-6-43J
Vocational Training
the initiative-to help Canadians establish themselves economically in our labour force here in Canada.

Even though we accept the principle of this bill we have to admit it is not exactly what we were expecting from the government in the way of helping those who are immediately confronted with unemployment. It has been said during the debate that Premier Lesage has admitted that the provinces have the responsibility in the field of unemployment. It is also a fact that when the minister was sitting on this side of the house he always claimed that unemployment was a matter for the federal authorities to deal with. He may have changed his mind since then, although I cannot understand how he and his colleagues could change their opinions in such a short space of time.
I remember that last year I admitted that unemployment was twofold in its nature. There is the unemployment which is caused by automation, presenting a problem for long range settlement, and there is the unemployment caused by economic changes taking place in this country. This latter kind of unemployment should be dealt with right away, because people are suffering at the present time. We know this bill will help those who are unemployed because of automation, and that it will help them to acquire the skills to take on new responsibilities in, say, three years time. But there is nothing here which deals with the immediate problem.
Much of the success of this measure is bound to depend on the success of our cooperation with the provinces. But has the government reached an understanding with the provinces? Nothing was said about this at the resolution stage, and nothing was said about it by the minister when he closed the debate on second reading a while ago. There is no doubt that in this legislation the federal government is placing a load on the shoulders of the provinces. It is ready to pay 50 per cent of the training, 25 per cent of the capital expenses incurred in organizing the schools, and so on. But I wonder if the provinces are ready to accept that load of 50 per cent on one hand and 25 per cent on the other. This question has not been discussed at all during this debate.

I am sure the hon. member does not mean what he says when he tells us that the federal government is prepared to pay only 25 per cent of the cost of the

Vocational Training
capital construction of buildings. I said that the federal government would pay 50 per cent but that if any project involving capital construction and equipment is undertaken before March 31, 1963, then the federal government would contribute an additional 25 per cent, which means that the federal government would contribute 75 per cent of the provincial contribution and leave the provincial government with 25 per cent to pay.

Even if it is an additional 25 per cent, there still remains a considerable expense to be carried by the province. Are the provinces ready to accept that expenditure of 75 per cent or 50 per cent, or even 25 per cent? Do they accept responsibility for this long range type of unemployment caused by automation? We have not heard on this point from any speaker on the government side. I really believe that the technical training systems we have in the province will not suffice to provide this additional training of the numbers who are in need of it. It is likely that the provinces will have to build new schools, or rent premises if there are any to be found. First of all, they will have to train the teachers, because I do not believe we have the necessary trained personnel at the moment to educate an additional several thousand people in each province. So this scheme is not complete, and in my opinion the hon. member for Essex East was right when he said the cost of this program should be carried 100 per cent by the federal government.
I do not dare present an amendment, because I know it would be declared irregular since it would add an additional expense to the treasury. Only a minister can do that. However, I hope and expect that the minister will look at this whole question from the standpoint I have indicated. Only a very small part of our unemployment today has been caused by automation. The rest of those who are unemployed in Canada are unemployed because the economic changes in the country are such that we cannot get rid of our surplus of goods. That is why factories have had to close or curtail their production; they have too much stock on hand.
This is not the responsibility of the provinces. At the present time, the main burden

with respect to unemployment is being carried by the municipalities. When I was in my office this morning someone showed me how the city of Hull had to pay $60 to one man in order that he might pay a month's rent, together with a few dollars to help him buy food for the family. There is certainly something in this situation which is not proper. We need something which is clearer and which would help the people of Canada at this time when they are actually in need, and they are not getting it from this bill. We admit that in three years, or five years, or six years, this measure will be of great help to this country, but it does not help people in the situation which confronts them at the present time and no bill has yet been presented which will provide anything to help the unemployed at this moment.
I hope, nevertheless, that this measure will pass, because we need it for a long range settlement. I hope the Minister of Labour will see that the government does bring in legislation much more applicable to the present situation faced by the unemployed all over this country. They need something immediately and I do not think that up to now the government has done anything in this domain.
I notice that the advisory council has been enlarged, and I do not know why this is needed. It was not explained by the minister. The minister announced that the hon. member for Cartier had discussed the matter but he never told the house why it was decided to enlarge the council. Will that help to solve the problem which faces us? I do not know. These are things which the minister can explain so that the committee may know exactly what this bill means. We know what it will accomplish in four, five or six years but not what it will accomplish at the present time. The government should devote its attention to introducing measures that will alleviate present suffering.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I was not able to be here on Wednesday when the main debate on second reading took place and it may be that one or two of the questions I should now like to put to the minister have been answered. I have not even had time to go through Hansard carefully. I hope the minister will accept my apology in advance if I am guilty of repetition.

There are a number of questions that have occurred to me about the departure that is now being taken in this bill. I thought perhaps I should put all my questions on clause 1 and if some of them relate to other clauses and might be more properly answered when we are dealing with those clauses the minister will be free to act accordingly.
The first question has to do primarily with the provision of additional facilities. As the minister knows, over a long period of time going back to 1910 the federal government has made contributions to some degree to the provision of facilities for vocational and technical education. There is nothing new about the principle and I am sure the minister never suggested there was but I have heard it suggested-and I do not profess to have any knowledge on this point-that in some of the provinces and specifically in Ontario there have been vocational training facilities provided in the high school system which facilities are not now in fact being used to capacity. I am sure some survey of this was made before the legislation was produced and I would like the minister to tell us just what the capacity is in each province, how many people could be trained in the existing institutions that have already been provided and in each province, as well, what the department's estimate is of the deficiency. I ask that because I assume the department has made some kind of estimate of how many places for additional pupils are really required in order to do the much larger job which I completely agree with the minister needs to be done.
I would even go so far as to say-and if the minister wants to make any political capital out of this he may-that it is perhaps unfortunate it was not started three years ago or even four years ago or even five years ago, but it was not; I mean, this expansion was not. It is true that over the years we have been making a very considerable contribution to these facilities but the tempo of that contribution was and still is entirely dependent on the provincial and local authorities.
I am not criticizing the government for that. I am not one of those who would advocate that the federal government should, of its own initiative, establish these institutions. I do not think it should. I believe that is a proper provincial function and that the way in which it was done by the previous government and which this government is proposing to continue on a somewhat larger scale is the right way to provide the facilities. However, what I think we ought to know before we actually accept the clauses of the bill is just how many cases there are in each
Vocational Training
province, how many pupils can be accommodated in the various categories of technical and vocational institutes now existing in each province, how many of these are being used at the present time, whether there are any that are not being used and if so in what regions they are, and also what the best estimate is-and I know, of course, it is only an estimate or perhaps an intelligent guess- of the additional places that it is thought will be required in each province to do the job adequately that now needs to be done.
The other thing I should like the minister to tell us is this. I recall that last session the federal government offered to contribute to the cost of training persons who are now unemployed. Would the minister tell us what advantage has thus far been taken of that offer and how many unemployed persons in each province are now receiving training under this joint federal-provincial arrangement.
It is my opinion and one I expressed at the last session which I understand has already been expressed in this debate by my colleagues in the Liberal party but which I want to reiterate myself that no part of the onus for the training of persons who are unemployed should be thrown upon the provincial or local authorities. I think we should regard this as a national problem in precisely the same way as we regarded the training and education of the veterans at the end of the war as a national problem. I am not saying that about young people who go into vocational schools and I hope the minister will not misunderstand me. I believe that is a proper function of the provinces. But in the case of persons who have been in the labour force but are now unemployed and who would benefit from training it seems to me there are several reasons why this should be done directly out of the federal treasury and not by the provinces. I should like briefly to place those reasons on the record.
The first is that we know now that every one of the schemes to alleviate unemployment presently in operation in fact gives the least help to the areas where there is the greatest concentration of unemployment and the most help to those areas where there is the least because the local authorities in those areas are best able to pay for the amelioration of the comparatively mild unemployment they have and as between the provinces, of course, the inequalities are very glaring as all the surveys we have had in every aspect of this field have shown. Therefore by saying that the federal government will pay only a part of the cost of the retraining of unemployed persons is to throw

Vocational Training
a highly unequal burden on different local authorities and different provinces.
There is another reason. There is no doubt that in some provinces the effect oi giving technical training to unemployed persons will be to lose that trained person to the province, that when the person becomes trained he will in many cases be more apt to get a job in some province other than the one in which he received the training. We want to maintain that mobility of labour in Canada and indeed in all conscience I think in these times we want to increase it but it is very hard, you know, to persuade the legislators of a province-say the province of Saskatchewan, for example-that they should contribute more money to train people so they will be enabled to come down and work in Ontario. It is quite understandable that they should feel that way. That, of course, was the great justification that Mr. St. Laurent gave for the university grants when they were established by the St. Laurent government but in this case the situation is even more compelling, it seems to me, because this is a problem that is national in character and now national in scope.
While undoubtedly the contribution the federal government is now prepared to make in this field is better than no contribution at all, it seems to me there is still a shirking of responsibility in this field and that the government should go the whole way and inaugurate a scheme similar to that which was followed in the case of the veterans after the war.
There is one special point about which I should like to ask the minister whether he has any information. He may not have but if he has I think it would be interesting to the committee to know whether there are any statistics available as to the number of persons who have over the past year or two received technical and vocational training and as to the increased employability and, indeed, the results in terms of increased employment for these persons because presumably a good deal of attention is being paid to that particular question.

That is right. With respect to co-operation between the provinces in this field I can cite a very good example. The pipe-line contractors, anticipating a great deal of work in the construction of pipe fines in the western provinces and particularly in Alberta in the coming year, indicated to us that there was a lack of specialized welders for this type of work. He said: Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be few and brief because the bill is a short one but I am sure that the Department of Justice will see the justice of the amendment contained therein. Perhaps I might explain that under the Penitentiary Act at the moment it is mandatory that an inmate -the word used is "convict" which I think is perhaps a wrong term-shall, except in the case of sickness, be kept in a cell by himself at night. That is section 66, subsection 4, of the present act. There is nothing in the act to permit the waiving of that provision and to allow for other arrangements than keeping the inmate in a cell by himself at night except in the case of sickness.
The purpose of my amendment is perhaps twofold. First, it is to prevent the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and every other official in the penitentiaries branch from continuing to break the law because they have been doing so for quite a number of years. I think they did so initially under force of circumstances as the result of overcrowding in various penitentiaries and latterly because modern penological attitudes

Penitentiary Act
are that it is not necessary to coniine people alone in cells at night and during the day. There is a more relaxed point oi view with regard to this matter. In any event, there is no doubt that the Minister of Justice and his predecessor were violating the Penitentiary Act for quite some time. I do not think there is anything too wrong about this situation but we certainly should not bring the law into disrespect by winking at it and thinking that it is not there.
The other purpose of the bill is to allow for flexibility on the part of penitentiary officials in determining whether it is necessary to keep an inmate in his cell or whether it would be more advantageous, more humanitarian and would tend more toward rehabilitation of the individual to permit him to sleep in what is commonly called a dormitory rather than behind bars in a cell with a lock on it.
I asked some questions about this matter in 1959 and perhaps I might put some of the information on the record to indicate the extent to which dormitories are used in penitentiaries under federal jurisdiction. The information was given on June 19, 1959, and is found at page 4984 of Hansard. In answer to one of my questions the reply was as follows:
Permanent dormitories have been constructed at the following institutions-Joyceville, 48 beds; federal training centre, 400 beds (6 beds per room); Collin's Bay, 2 dormitories (50 beds each); Kingston, 1 dormitory (42 beds); St. Vincent de Paul, 1 dormitory (120 beds); British Columbia, 2 dormitories (58 beds each). Total: 826.
In addition, it is pointed out that temporary dormitories were established either in shop space or corridors in several prisons, which provided a total of 481 beds. The situation as of December 31, 1958 was that there were 1,171 inmates sleeping in dormitories contrary to what the act provides, namely that each man shall be confined by himself in a cell at night.
I think the practice of allowing this flexibility on the part of wardens and other penitentiary officials in selecting individual inmates or groups of inmates, depending upon circumstances, to be placed in dormitories rather than to be confined in cells is a good one and that the law is wrong and should be changed if we want to keep up with the practice both from the humanitarian point of view and from the point of view of having regard to the strict meaning of the law.
This matter was raised during another session and I notice there is an indication in the speech from the throne that we can expect amendments to the Penitentiary Act sponsored by the government at this session. Knowing something about the attitude of the 
present Minister of Justice so far as penology is concerned, I would rather expect that he would have taken steps to deal with this point, whether or not in these words does not matter, in the bill that he will be presenting later this session. This is only guesswork on my part but I certainly hope that it does so.
If the provision in my bill is in essence contained in any way in the bill forecast in the speech from the throne it may be that my bill comes in conflict with the rule about anticipation and if that is the case I am quite prepared to withdraw this proposal and not have it stand on the order paper because I would not want the minister to run afoul of the rules when his bill is introduced. However, we can cross that bridge when we come to it. At the moment I simply say that from a humanitarian and penological point of view I believe the wardens and prison officials should be given this statutory authority.
To some degree it has something to do in my view with the great need to rehabilitate the inmates of our prisons and ensure that they do not become recidivists once they are released. The approach of allowing inmates to sleep in dormitories rather than being confined in cells behind bars all night and half the day is much preferable and I hope that this amendment will be given the endorsation of the house either now or at a later stage.

In some of the older institutions it is the practice for people to pick up their meals and carry them into the cell. However, there should be some place where the man or woman can, if he or she chooses, have that degree of privacy which I think is necessary. Surely, one of our aims is to preserve the dignity of the human being and this cannot be done unless there is some opportunity for them to be alone.
I recall, Mr. Speaker, on one occasion visiting a penitentiary where the inmates, with the material they had available, had arranged their quarters so that they looked as little as possible like institutional cells. It was extremely interesting to see the effect they had created. On another occasion, I had the privilege of visiting one man's cell in Kingston penitentiary and viewing the paintings which he had done. These had been artistically arranged around the very small walls of the cells. It has always seemed to me that the cell is the one area in an institution where an inmate can temporarily shut himself away from the institutional life, and I do think he benefits from this opportunity.
I believe that our Department of Justice suffers greatly from a lack of the necessary facilities for properly segregating those who are taken into institutions. I feel that to change the law which now demands a private cell for each inmate is a mistake. I realize that there are times when it is necessary for the warden who is in charge of the institution to use whatever accommodation he has. have been interested in this question of penology, Mr. Speaker, for a great many years. I must say that my experience in visiting penal institutions is certainly different from that which has just been described by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Allmark). I try to visit the penal institution in British Columbia not less than twice a year.
I was most interested some two or three years ago when the warden took me around, showed me the dormitory set-up which had been established and explained how it operated. I spent a number of hours in talking to the men who occupied those dormitories at night. They were not only exceedingly happy about the new arrangement but they felt that they were being honoured in that they had been selected and had been given the responsibility and the opportunity of being together on a social basis instead of being locked up in a cell for many hours every night of their term. May I just add also that this matter of a single cell can have extremely serious harmful effects and repercussions on many individuals, especially if they have any tendency whatsoever to claustrophobia.
I think we must admit that the inauguration of this new policy of dormitories in the penal institutions came about because of necessity in that there was not available the required cell accommodation as laid down in the Penitentiary Act. Hence the actual wording of the law had to be broken and it was broken by the wardens of penitentiaries with the permission, of course, of the commissioner and the minister.
I want to say that all those who were permitted this, shall we say, togetherness on a social basis in the dormitory system are always those who are the best behaved in the penitentiary and are nearly always those who are going to be discharged from the institution in a short period of time. They are carefully selected and are carefully watched. Not only are they under the close supervision of the officers of the institution, but they themselves exercise a great deal of self-discipline.
In the dormitories that I have visited they have their own committee to see that all regulations are complied with because they do not want to lose the right to stay in a dormitory. If any rule is broken the men themselves are the first to have a real heart to heart talk with the offender. As a result of what I have been told by those with whom I have spoken, if there is one thing a man does not want to lose, it is his right to be in a dormitory; and if there is one thing he does not want, it is to be sent back to the solitary confinement of a cell.

In the institutions which I have visited and which have the dormitory system I have heard of only two occasions when any individual ever abused the privilege. One was handled speedily by the men and by the authorities and the offender was sent back to a solitary cell. The other was an interesting incident. By some cute method a still was established in a kitchen, material was introduced into the dormitory and for a week the guards could not find where it was. Speedy action was taken there also.
Those are the only occasions over the years on which I have ever heard of anything happening because the men were given this privilege. I think it is a most needful step forward and a most progressive move. It is appreciated by the men concerned. They apply to go to the dormitory. They are not constrained. They may stay in a private cell if they wish to do so. However, most of them do not wish to do so. It is therefore only natural and reasonable that at this time we should consider the advisability and, I would almost say, the inevitability of correcting the statute so that the procedure which is now being followed is in accordance with the actual wording of the Penitentiary Act.

speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), Mr. Speaker, I have visited both maximum and minimum security penitentiaries. Like him, I have found that the dormitory system of handling inmates has a great many advantages over the cell block type of accommodation that is found in the maximum security institutions.
In my constituency the Department of Justice recently established a minimum security institution. I may say to the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Allmark) that I agree with him wholeheartedly in my feeling that the people in my area are happy to have the present institution located there and would be most happy to see it extended and enlarged.
I have visited the maximum security institution at Dorchester and, as the hon. member for Kingston pointed out, I have also noted that many prisoners take a great deal of pride in their individual cells-I refer to those who have an individual cell-they do carry out many innovations that would indicate they are the only places they can call home. They put up curtains and do other small things that would indicate their interest in these cells.
In my opinion, the cell block situation is necessary in some instances. However, in many instances it is a burden on the inmate and holds back his possible return to society.

For one thing, the cell block type of institution forces the warden and his officials to go through a number of procedures that are extremely time consuming. This requirement means that there is little opportunity for the inmate to do as much gainful work as might otherwise be the case. It also means that the inmate spends a great many hours of the day in the cell. This could lead to a good deal of meditation and probably brooding, the feeling that society in general is against him and that he has not been given the chance to which he feels he is entitled.
In visiting the minimum security institution at Springhill and in talking with the inmates I found an altogether different attitude among those inmates. There was an enlightened attitude on their part, that society did not altogether detest them for what they had done. They did not altogether feel that their mistakes could not be rectified. Their attitude is that they are being given a chance to live, sleep and eat together and a chance to get back into society at an earlier date than otherwise would be possible.
Also when I visited these dormitories I found the beds were of a very good quality, with foam-rubber mattresses and foam-rubber pillows. Each bed in the dormitory that I visited was very clean and very well kept. Indeed, there was the indication that there was a great deal of pride on the part of the inmates of this dormitory.
I agree with what the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) has said about the individual inmate's attitude towards being allowed to stay in dormitories, sleep there and associate with his fellow inmates. I think it is true that if one inmate were to do something against the regulations the others there would very quickly see to it that this breaking of the regulations was corrected immediately.
I also think we must point out that the matter of space, the fact that a man is not looking at three walls and bars, is a tremendous asset to him later when he must return to society. In each of these dormitories there is not only the bed, but there is a desk. There is also a small cloakroom, or cabinet, in which he can put his belongings. Each cabinet has a lock on it and for all intents and purposes his personal belongings are located there.
The dormitory is not only his sleeping quarters; it is a place in which after a day's work the inmates can get together and discuss their mutual difficulties and the matters they have in common in a free and easy atmosphere. There is nothing more forbidding, to my way of thinking, than to go into a maximum security institution and see an individual caged like an animal in a two by
Penitentiary Act
four where he cannot help but feel that no one cares about him. As far as I am concerned, there is a great deal of merit in the type of amendment proposed in Bill No. C-2.
Naturally, all inmates would not be interested in this type of quarters. Some, for one reason or other, do not feel they can trust themselves in a minimum security institution, especially living in a dormitory where there are no bars and no real outward appearances of guards and all the other things that are associated with maximum security institutions. I feel those people must of necessity remain in cells because they cannot place upon themselves the responsibility that would be their's if they entered the minimum security type of institution.
However, for those who have indicated they are willing to accept the responsibility that goes with the minimum security type of institution, who long for association with others, who have indicated they are almost ready to again enter society, this type of dormitory living is an absolute necessity today.
We have learned that it is cheaper from the taxpayers' point of view to provide the minimum security type of institution and to parole inmates as quickly as they indicate it is possible. We have also learned that this type of dormitory institution prepares those who for one reason or another have found it necessary to break the laws of our country, have been caught and must pay the penalty, and who have realized the folly of their ways-those who have indicated that they are now willing to return to society as soon as we are willing to allow them to do so. This dormitory type of association is, in my opinion, the best means of achieving this.
I feel that this government more than any other has indicated the enlightened approach to penology that I feel Canadians generally have indicated they are willing to accept. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has undertaken at a very rapid pace the construction of minimum security institutions throughout this country.
I feel that the dormitory system, or the minimum security system of handling inmates, is one that will benefit not only the taxpayer but society generally and that we will as a result of our actions in this regard have better citizens and a better Canada.
