Mr. Speaker, unlike many members of this house, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who I heard speaking a few moments ago, I have never had the opportunity nor-and I must confess that it may be a deficiency on my part-have I ever expressed a desire to visit a penitentiary

Penitentiary Act
or provincial jail. Perhaps-in fact, almost certainly-I alone of all the members of this house have had the experience of being incarcerated, although not in a prison. Having been subject to confinement for almost three years during the second world war as a prisoner of war, I think I can understand some of the feelings of a man who is held against his will in confinement, under regimentation, controlled by armed guards and, on occasions, being fired at by guards. I know something of the inner desire of a human being for alternatives when he is living under those conditions.
There we did not live in isolation. On the contrary, we were herded, 20 to 28 of us, into small rooms and after a time one felt that the greatest boon which could be given would be to have a cell or a single room of one's own in which to sleep at night so as to get away from the press of one's fellow-men. I do not know whether I can succeed in describing the effect of spending 24 hours a day in the constant company of one's fellows. It is not possible to get away from them, whether one is sleeping, eating, or out for a walk within the limiting confines of a prison camp. To be alone by oneself even to think was something almost unimaginable and, in the end, when release came, one had almost lost any capacity for independent action. We did not know what to do with ourselves.
Nevertheless, I agree in principle with the aims and motives of this bill-that in selective cases men might be given the privilege of sleeping in a dormitory room. I understand the argument that this might be better for the men themselves, as well as for the purposes of administration, and I fully appreciate what the hon. member for Vancouver East said about the esteem in which this privilege was held. However, I would not wish to see men compulsorily kept in a dormitory for a lengthy period.
Some people object to the idea that a man should be isolated at night during the whole period of a lengthy sentence, and I would think that within the regulations it might be possible for these men to be treated in the way suggested. I do not believe that in a minimum security prison everybody should be put in a dormitory, because I can tell hon. members from my own experience that there is nothing so oppressive as constant contact, 24 hours a day, seven days a week and 12 months of the year with one's fellow men. There is nothing so soul-destroying. You get to know the idiosyncrasies of everyone: you can almost tell from what corner of the room snores will come during the night; who is grinding his teeth, who will have to go out to relieve himself. Worse, there is the

bitter snapping, the quarrels. On the other hand, such conditions may help some persons to become more tolerant of the idiosyncrasies of others.
While I approve the principle of this bill I may mention that it would have the effect of amending a section of the act which I read, almost with nostalgia since it is written in the same style, with the same brevity and, I would say, callousness as the orders which governed confinement that I experienced. It may be possible, within the regulations, for the minister, the commissioner or a warden in the administration of his prison or penitentiary to make a change in the nature of the confinement of an individual. I would hope that such consideration could be given to this proposal in the light of the administrative requirements of our penitentiary system along with many other types of change, and I am only speaking theoretically about other types of change; perhaps this can be done within the administrative requirements of our present system.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR USE OF DORMITORIES BY INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple bill and we have had a very good discussion. I think the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) deserves a great deal of credit for bringing this question forward. Briefly, the measure would have the effect of making it non-mandatory for those in authority to segregate inmates at night, that is, confine them in solitary, as it were, although I do not mean in the sense of punishment. With the intention of the bill expressed simply in that way, I think most hon. members would agree. The actual explanation accompanying the bill should probably be placed on the record:
The purpose of the proposed amendment is to give the minister and the commissioner power to relax the law in proper cases and thus authorize the warden to keep selected groups of convicts together in dormitories at night.
The speech from the throne of November 17 contains this sentence:
You will also be asked to revise the Penitentiaries Act to bring it into accord with my minister's policies of correctional reform.
I think it would be reasonable to suppose that the principle which this bill embodies will certainly be contained in this amendment when it comes forward. The question of correctional planning and prison reform does deserve some consideration. The hon. member for Skeena suggested that the law was being broken but I believe that if an examination were made of the Penitentiary Act it would reveal other sections of that legislation which gives the authority to those with responsibility to permit some dormitory activity in the case of overcrowding.

I agree with the thoughts expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who has long been interested in penology and was keenly interested in the comments made by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Allmark) who has close contact with our largest penitentiary, although that hon. gentleman did place some reservations on his words. If I may attempt to sum up what was said by all who participated in the debate I would say that some were more extreme in expressing their views about the desirability of togetherness and others expressed reservations about getting away from the practice of confinement of a solitary nature such as in cells. I feel it would be undesirable to go to either extreme and therefore merely making action non-mandatory would probably have the desired effect.
I have not been too interested in the subject of prison reform and related problems but recently it was my privilege to visit two or three of our larger penitentiaries. I am aware that this is an extremely pertinent subject nowadays and as a result of my visits I have become highly conscious of the plight of the prisoners. I am, of course, thinking seriously of their problems and of the new correctional planning the government proposes to undertake in this regard under the leadership of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). I think it is important for hon. members to visit penitentiaries and acquaint themselves with the subject of prison reform and the problems in connection therewith because hon. members have a responsibility for our inmates. I was interested in learning that in 1873 some of the rules and regulations of penitentiary conduct were, and I quote briefly:
Convicts are to labour diligently and preserve unbroken silence. They must not exchange a word with one another under any pretence whatever.
They must not exchange looks, wink, laugh, nod or gesticulate to each other.
They must approach their keepers in the most respectful manner and be brief in their communication. They are not to speak to or address their keepers on any subject such as relates to their work, duty or wants.
They are not on any occasion nor under any pretence to speak to any person who does not belong to the prison.
They are not to stop work nor suffer their attention to be drawn from it. They are not to gaze at visitors when passing through the prison nor sing, dance, whistle, run, jump nor do anything which may have the slightest tendency to disturb the harmony or to contravene the rules and regulations of the prison.
For the wilful violation of any of these duties corporal punishment will be instantly inflicted.
We have come a long way from the regulations of 1873 and as this bill proposes I think it is desirable to ensure that prison rules and regulations are in keeping with contemporary standards of human decency.
Business of the House
In my visits there was a great deal more cleanliness apparent in the dormitories although I reserve my full approval of dormitories to minimum security type inmates or at least those who are due to be released. I feel they should be taken from lone cells and placed in dormitories for a period in order to straighten out their thinking, work out their associations and reactions and make it easier for them to adjust to society.
It was interesting to note some of the benefits which I felt were apparent as a result of this dormitory activity. In one large penitentiary we noticed a great deal of interest in sports and other parts of their program. When we approached the grievance committees many prisoners wanted to know if it would be possible to get Rocket Richard and Jean Belliveau to visit them. This was a dormitory activity they were thinking about and planning. I think the dormitory suggestion has great merit in this regard.
Another interesting observation I made in one dormitory-style minimum security prison related to the selection of television programs and channels available on the television set provided for their use. In a manner such as we would all likely adopt the group decided to pick out the programs that were most popular to watch for the evening. I found it interesting to learn that the most popular program, the favourite of all concerned, was the one about the R.C.M.P. Incidents of this nature help us to appreciate the human relations aspect of prison life.
I have nothing further to say at this time and had only two purposes in rising. I believe this debate has served a useful purpose in interesting hon. members in this new thinking with respect to prison reform. Those who have spoken did so on the basis of knowledge, interest and perhaps on the basis of personal visits. This is something we might consider undertaking through the Department of Justice and the visit of members of parliament to large prison institutions. This would be planned and I suppose they would know we were coming and we could talk to the grievance committees and find out what the inmates had on their minds.
I am sure this is a good measure and that something along the lines of the principle involved here will be forthcoming at the appropriate time. May I call it six o'clock?
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the house leader what the plans are for next week?

Well, Mr. Speaker, I must say I greatly appreciate the assistance of the hon. member for Halifax.

I was recently looking back at an earlier year, Mr. Speaker, when it was not the practice for hon. members on the other side of the house to ask what the business was. The house leader simply used to get up and announce it.
On Monday we will be in the committee stage on the bill relating to technical and vocational training and I hope perhaps we will finish it. That will be followed by the resolution concerning the productivity council. The third item as I mentioned yesterday would be the resolution on veterans pensions. That business will hold for Monday and Tuesday, I expect.
Does the minister have any additional suggestions in case that should not take the whole of Monday and Tuesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: At any time the house sees fit to do it we have several committees to be set up; procedure, Indian affairs and research in that order. I did suggest yesterday that on Wednesday we might reach supplementary estimates but I also said that would depend on the progress made by the house on the other pieces of legislation.
Does the minister hope to get the supplementary estimates through before the Christmas recess?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Exactly, and I had hoped to get the committee stage of the bill on technical and vocational training through today which would have enabled us for certain to proceed with the supplementary estimates next week.
